claim: East Asians experience worse metabolic health outcomes compared to other ethnic groups at lower body mass indices.
source: East Asians (EAs) experience worse metabolic health outcomes compared to other ethnic groups at lower body mass indices
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about health disparities.

claim: The IDEO cohort study included 46 lean and obese East Asian and White participants living in the San Francisco Bay Area.
source: We conducted a multi-omic study of 46 lean and obese East Asian and White participants living in the San Francisco Bay Area
evidence: The study design and participant numbers are explicitly stated in the abstract.

claim: There are marked differences in bacterial richness between East Asian and White subjects.
source: revealing marked differences between ethnic groups in bacterial richness and community structure
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: White individuals were enriched for the mucin-degrading Akkermansia muciniphila.
source: White individuals were enriched for the mucin-degrading Akkermansia muciniphila.
evidence: This specific bacterial enrichment is stated in the abstract.

claim: East Asian subjects had increased levels of multiple bacterial phyla.
source: East Asian subjects had increased levels of multiple bacterial phyla
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by data in the results.

claim: East Asian subjects had increased levels of fermentative pathways detected by metagenomics.
source: East Asian subjects had increased levels of multiple bacterial phyla, fermentative pathways detected by metagenomics
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from metagenomic analysis.

claim: East Asian subjects had increased levels of the short-chain fatty acid end-products acetate, propionate, and isobutyrate.
source: East Asian subjects had increased levels of multiple bacterial phyla, fermentative pathways detected by metagenomics, and the short-chain fatty acid end-products acetate, propionate, and isobutyrate.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by metabolomics data.

claim: Differences in the gut microbiota between East Asian and White subjects could not be explained by dietary intake.
source: Differences in the gut microbiota between the East Asian and White subjects could not be explained by dietary intake
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract based on dietary analysis.

claim: Differences in the gut microbiota between East Asian and White subjects were more pronounced in lean individuals.
source: Differences in the gut microbiota between the East Asian and White subjects could not be explained by dietary intake, were more pronounced in lean individuals
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by stratified analysis in the results.

claim: Differences in the gut microbiota between East Asian and White subjects were associated with current geographical location.
source: Differences in the gut microbiota between the East Asian and White subjects could not be explained by dietary intake, were more pronounced in lean individuals, and were associated with current geographical location.
evidence: This association is stated in the abstract and supported by geographical analysis.

claim: Microbiome transplantations into germ-free mice demonstrated stable diet- and host genotype-independent differences between the gut microbiotas of East Asian and White individuals.
source: Microbiome transplantations into germ-free mice demonstrated stable diet- and host genotype-independent differences between the gut microbiotas of East Asian and White individuals
evidence: This experimental finding is stated in the abstract and supported by mouse experiments.

claim: Ethnicity-associated differences in the gut microbiota differentially impact host body composition in mice.
source: Microbiome transplantations into germ-free mice demonstrated stable diet- and host genotype-independent differences between the gut microbiotas of East Asian and White individuals that differentially impact host body composition.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by body composition measurements in mice.

claim: Culture-independent surveys have emphasized differences in gut microbial community structure between countries.
source: Culture-independent surveys have emphasized differences in gut microbial community structure between countries (Hehemann et al., 2010; Vangay et al., 2018; Yatsunenko et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Diet is a common hypothesis for geographical variations in the gut microbiota.
source: Diet is a common hypothesis for geographical variations in the gut microbiota (De Filippo et al., 2010; Devoto et al., 2019)
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Self-identified race/ethnicity integrates the broader national or cultural tradition of a given social group.
source: Self-identified race/ethnicity (SIRE) provides a useful alternative, as it integrates the broader national or cultural tradition of a given social group
evidence: This is a conceptual statement about the meaning of SIRE.

claim: Self-identified race/ethnicity is closely tied to both dietary intake and genetic ancestry.
source: Self-identified race/ethnicity (SIRE) provides a useful alternative, as it integrates the broader national or cultural tradition of a given social group and is closely tied to both dietary intake and genetic ancestry.
evidence: This is a conceptual statement about the relationships between SIRE and other factors.

claim: Multiple studies have reported associations between the gut microbiota and ethnicity in China.
source: Multiple studies have reported associations between the gut microbiota and ethnicity in China (Khine et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Multiple studies have reported associations between the gut microbiota and ethnicity in the Netherlands.
source: Multiple studies have reported associations between the gut microbiota and ethnicity in China (Khine et al., 2019), the Netherlands (Deschasaux et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Multiple studies have reported associations between the gut microbiota and ethnicity in Singapore.
source: Multiple studies have reported associations between the gut microbiota and ethnicity in China (Khine et al., 2019), the Netherlands (Deschasaux et al., 2018), Singapore (Xu et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Multiple studies have reported associations between the gut microbiota and ethnicity in the United States.
source: Multiple studies have reported associations between the gut microbiota and ethnicity in China (Khine et al., 2019), the Netherlands (Deschasaux et al., 2018), Singapore (Xu et al., 2020), and the United States (Brooks et al., 2018; Sordillo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A recent study of Asian immigrants suggested that once an individual relocates to a new country, the microbiota rapidly assumes the structure of the country of residence.
source: In contrast, a recent study of Asian immigrants suggested that once an individual relocates to a new country, the microbiota rapidly assumes the structure of the country of residence (Vangay et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: East Asian subjects are more likely to develop health-related metabolic complications at lower body mass index compared to their White counterparts.
source: For example, East Asian (EA) subjects are more likely to develop health-related metabolic complications at lower body mass index (BMI) compared to their White (W) counterparts (Gu et al., 2006; Zheng et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Asian Americans have persistent ethnic differences in metabolic phenotypes following immigration.
source: Moreover, Asian Americans have persistent ethnic differences in metabolic phenotypes following immigration (Jih et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Asian Americans have a decoupling of BMI from total body fat percentage.
source: Moreover, Asian Americans have persistent ethnic differences in metabolic phenotypes following immigration (Jih et al., 2014), including a decoupling of BMI from total body fat percentage (Alba et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Human genetic polymorphisms may play a role in ethnic differences in fat accrual.
source: Human genetic polymorphisms may play a role (Wen et al., 2010; Xiang et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Putative alleles associated with ethnic differences in fat accrual are often shared between members of different ethnic groups.
source: however, putative alleles are often shared between members of different ethnic groups (Gravel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The gut microbiome might offer a possible explanation for differences in metabolic disease rates across ethnic groups.
source: The gut microbiome might offer a possible explanation for differences in metabolic disease rates across ethnic groups (He et al., 2018)
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: There has been a relative scarcity of microbiome studies examining ethnic differences in metabolic disease.
source: but there has been a relative scarcity of microbiome studies in this area (Gaulke and Sharpton, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Principal coordinates analysis of PhILR Euclidean distances from 16S-seq data revealed a subtle but significant separation between the gut microbiotas of EA and W subjects (p=0.006, R2=0.046).
source: Principal coordinates analysis of PhILR Euclidean distances from 16S-seq data (Supplementary file 1B, n=22 EA, 24 W subjects) revealed a subtle but significant separation between the gut microbiotas of EA and W subjects (p=0.006, R2=0.046, ADONIS; Figure 1A).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1A showing the PCoA plot.

claim: Statistical significance of the separation between EA and W gut microbiotas was robust to the distance metric used.
source: Statistical significance was robust to the distance metric used (Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to supplementary data.

claim: Bacterial diversity was significantly higher in W individuals across three distinct metrics: Faith's phylogenetic diversity, amplicon sequence variant (ASV) richness, and Shannon diversity.
source: Bacterial diversity was significantly higher in W individuals across three distinct metrics: Faith's phylogenetic diversity, amplicon sequence variant (ASV) richness, and Shannon diversity (Figure 1B).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1B showing the diversity metrics.

claim: Six bacterial phyla were significantly different between ethnicities.
source: Six bacterial phyla were significantly different between ethnicities (Figure 1C)
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1C showing phylum-level abundances.

claim: Only one phylum, Verrucomicrobiota, was significantly enriched in W subjects.
source: of which only one phylum, Verrucomicrobiota, was significantly enriched in W subjects.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and can be seen in Figure 1C.

claim: Blautia, Bacteroides, and Streptococcus were significantly enriched in EA subjects at the genus level.
source: Several significant differences were detectable at the genus level (Figure 1D–E), including Blautia, Bacteroides, and Streptococcus which were significantly enriched in EA subjects.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1E showing genus-level differential abundance.

claim: Two ASVs were significantly different between ethnicities: Blautia obeum and a Streptococcus species, both enriched in EA subjects.
source: We also identified two ASVs that were significantly different between ethnicities: Blautia obeum and a Streptococcus species, both enriched in EA subjects (Figure 1F).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1F showing ASV-level differential abundance.

claim: There were no significant differences between ethnicities in 16S rRNA copy number.
source: There were no significant differences between ethnicities in 16S rRNA copy number (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: B. obeum (ASV1) was the top contributor to the random forest classifier distinguishing EA and W subjects.
source: B. obeum (ASV1) was the top contributor to the resulting classifier, followed by Anaerostipes hadrus (ASV45) and then Streptococcus parasanguinis (ASV110) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PhILR transformed phylogenetic nodes achieved a higher area under the curve compared to ASVs in the random forest classifier.
source: Both classifiers demonstrated the ability to distinguish between ethnic groups, with PhILR transformed phylogenetic nodes achieving a higher area under the curve compared to ASVs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D showing ROC curves.

claim: The majority (18/23) of the top ASVs identified by the classifier were also significantly different between ethnicities.
source: The majority (18/23) of the top ASVs identified by our classifier were also significantly different between ethnicities (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Metagenomic sequencing provided independent confirmation of differences in the gut microbiome between ethnicities.
source: Metagenomic sequencing provided independent confirmation of differences in the gut microbiome between ethnicities (Supplementary file 1B, n=21 EA, 24 W subjects).
evidence: This is stated in the text as a finding from metagenomic analysis.

claim: A difference in the gut microbiomes between ethnicities was detected based upon metagenomic species abundances (p=0.003, R2=0.047).
source: Consistent with our 16S-seq analysis, we detected a difference in the gut microbiomes between ethnicities based upon metagenomic species abundances (p=0.003, R2=0.047, ADONIS, Figure 2A)
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2A showing the PCoA plot.

claim: A difference in the gut microbiomes between ethnicities was detected based upon gene families (p=0.029, R2=0.036).
source: we detected a difference in the gut microbiomes between ethnicities based upon metagenomic species abundances (p=0.003, R2=0.047, ADONIS, Figure 2A) and gene families (p=0.029, R2=0.036, ADONIS).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text based on metagenomic analysis.

claim: Ethnicity explained more variation in species abundances than a selection of demographic, laboratory, lifestyle, and metabolic metadata.
source: Ethnicity explained more variation in species abundances than a selection of demographic, laboratory, lifestyle, and metabolic metadata (Figure 2B).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2B showing PERMANOVA results.

claim: Akkermansia and an unspecified Erysipelotrichaceae genera were significantly different between ethnicities and elevated in W individuals.
source: Genera that were found to be significantly different between ethnicities in our metagenomic data included Akkermansia and an unspecified Erysipelotrichaceae genera (Figure 2D) elevated in W individuals.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2D showing genus-level differential abundance.

claim: Four bacterial species were significantly different between ethnicities in metagenomic data: W individuals had higher levels of A. muciniphila, Bacteroidales bacterium ph8, and Roseburia hominis, and lower levels of Ruminococcus gnavus, compared to EA individuals.
source: Four bacterial species were significantly different between ethnicities in our metagenomic data: W individuals had higher levels of A. muciniphila, Bacteroidales bacterium ph8, and Roseburia hominis, and lower levels of Ruminococcus gnavus, compared to EA individuals (Figure 2E).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2E showing species-level differential abundance.

claim: Metabolite profiles were more strongly associated with ethnicity (p=0.008, R2=0.128) than community structure (R2=0.029–0.055) or gene abundance (p=0.029, R2=0.036).
source: Metabolite profiles were more strongly associated with ethnicity (p=0.008, R2=0.128, ADONIS; Figure 3A) than community structure (R2=0.029–0.055, ADONIS; Supplementary file 1C) or gene abundance (p=0.029, R2=0.036, ADONIS).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3A showing the PCoA plot of metabolite profiles.

claim: EA subjects had elevated levels of the branched-chain amino acid valine.
source: Feature annotations revealed elevated levels of the branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) valine and the short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) acetate and propionate in EA subjects (Figure 3B and Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3B showing metabolite levels.

claim: EA subjects had elevated levels of the short-chain fatty acids acetate and propionate.
source: Feature annotations revealed elevated levels of the branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) valine and the short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) acetate and propionate in EA subjects (Figure 3B and Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3B showing metabolite levels.

claim: W subjects had higher levels of proline, formate, alanine, xanthine, and hypoxanthine.
source: In contrast, proline, formate, alanine, xanthine, and hypoxanthine were found at higher levels in W subjects (Figure 3B).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3B showing metabolite levels.

claim: EA subjects had significantly higher levels of stool acetate.
source: Confirming our NMR data, EA subjects had significantly higher levels of stool acetate (Figure 3C)
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3C showing GC-MS quantification.

claim: EA subjects had significantly higher levels of stool propionate.
source: Confirming our NMR data, EA subjects had significantly higher levels of stool acetate (Figure 3C) and propionate (Figure 3D)
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3D showing GC-MS quantification.

claim: EA subjects had significantly higher levels of stool isobutyrate.
source: Isobutyrate (which was not detected by NMR) was also significantly higher in EA subjects (Figure 3E).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3E showing GC-MS quantification.

claim: There was no significant difference in BCAAs between EA and W subjects.
source: however, we did not detect any significant differences in BCAAs or bile acids (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no significant difference in bile acids between EA and W subjects.
source: however, we did not detect any significant differences in BCAAs or bile acids (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A targeted re-analysis of metagenomic data revealed a significant enrichment in 'pyruvate fermentation to butanoate' pathway (p=0.023, fold-difference=2.216).
source: In agreement with these metabolite levels, a targeted re-analysis of our metagenomic data revealed a significant enrichment in two SCFA-related pathways: 'pyruvate fermentation to butanoate' (p=0.023, fold-difference=2.216)
evidence: This finding is stated in the text based on metagenomic pathway analysis.

claim: A targeted re-analysis of metagenomic data revealed a significant enrichment in 'superpathway of Clostridium acetobutylicum acidogenic fermentation' pathway (p=0.023, fold-difference=2.182).
source: In agreement with these metabolite levels, a targeted re-analysis of our metagenomic data revealed a significant enrichment in two SCFA-related pathways: 'pyruvate fermentation to butanoate' (p=0.023, fold-difference=2.216) and 'superpathway of Clostridium acetobutylicum acidogenic fermentation' (p=0.023, fold-difference=2.182).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text based on metagenomic pathway analysis.

claim: Gut bacterial richness in W individuals was significantly associated with BMI.
source: Consistent with prior work (Le Chatelier et al., 2013; Turnbaugh et al., 2008), we found that gut bacterial richness in W individuals was significantly associated with both BMI (Figure 4A)
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4A showing the correlation.

claim: Gut bacterial richness in W individuals was significantly associated with body fat percentage.
source: Consistent with prior work (Le Chatelier et al., 2013; Turnbaugh et al., 2008), we found that gut bacterial richness in W individuals was significantly associated with both BMI (Figure 4A) and body fat percentage (Figure 4B).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4B showing the correlation.

claim: The associations between gut bacterial richness and BMI/body fat percentage were undetectable in EA subjects.
source: Remarkably, these associations were undetectable in EA subjects (Figure 4A and B)
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4A and B showing no correlation in EA subjects.

claim: A negative correlation between Shannon diversity and BMI was detected in EA subjects.
source: even when other metrics of bacterial diversity were used (Figure 4—figure supplement 1),with the single exception of a negative correlation between Shannon diversity and BMI in EA subjects (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The differences between ethnic groups in the gut microbiota were driven by lean individuals.
source: Re-analysis of our data separating lean and obese individuals revealed that the previously observed differences between ethnic groups were driven by lean individuals.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text based on stratified analysis.

claim: Lean W subjects had significantly higher bacterial diversity compared to lean EA individuals.
source: Compared to lean EA individuals, lean W subjects had significantly higher bacterial diversity (Figure 4C)
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4C showing diversity metrics.

claim: Lean W subjects had more marked differences in gut microbial community structure compared to lean EA individuals (p=0.0003, R2=0.122).
source: Compared to lean EA individuals, lean W subjects had significantly higher bacterial diversity (Figure 4C) and more marked differences in gut microbial community structure (p=0.0003, R2=0.122, ADONIS; Figure 4D)
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4D showing the PCoA plot.

claim: Lean W subjects had more marked differences in metabolite profiles compared to lean EA individuals (p=0.010, R2=0.293).
source: Compared to lean EA individuals, lean W subjects had significantly higher bacterial diversity (Figure 4C) and more marked differences in gut microbial community structure (p=0.0003, R2=0.122, ADONIS; Figure 4D) and metabolite profiles (p=0.010, R2=0.293, ADONIS; Figure 4E).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4E showing the PCoA plot.

claim: Obese W versus EA individuals were not different in gut microbial community structure or metabolite profiles.
source: By contrast, obese W versus EA individuals were not different across any of these metrics (Figure 4C–E), except for lower Shannon diversity in obese EA compared to W individuals (Figure 4C).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4C-E.

claim: Obese EA individuals had lower Shannon diversity compared to obese W individuals.
source: By contrast, obese W versus EA individuals were not different across any of these metrics (Figure 4C–E), except for lower Shannon diversity in obese EA compared to W individuals (Figure 4C).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4C.

claim: 5/6 phyla that were differentially abundant between ethnicities were also significantly different between lean EA and W individuals.
source: We also detected differences in the gut microbiotas of lean EA and W individuals at the phylum (Figure 5A) and genus (Figure 5B) levels that were largely consistent with our original analysis of the full data set (Figure 1C and E).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5A showing phylum-level differences.

claim: More modest differences in the gut microbiota between ethnicities were observed in obese subjects.
source: More modest differences in the gut microbiota between ethnicities were observed in obese subjects (Figure 5A and C).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5A and C.

claim: Diabetes was significantly associated with variance in the PhILR Euclidean distances.
source: Consistent with prior studies (Falony et al., 2016), PERMANOVA analysis of our full 16S-seq data set revealed that diabetes (Forslund et al., 2015), age (Ghosh et al., 2020), metformin use (Wu et al., 2017), and statin intake (Vieira-Silva et al., 2020) were significantly associated with variance in the PhILR Euclidean distances (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Age was significantly associated with variance in the PhILR Euclidean distances.
source: Consistent with prior studies (Falony et al., 2016), PERMANOVA analysis of our full 16S-seq data set revealed that diabetes (Forslund et al., 2015), age (Ghosh et al., 2020), metformin use (Wu et al., 2017), and statin intake (Vieira-Silva et al., 2020) were significantly associated with variance in the PhILR Euclidean distances (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Metformin use was significantly associated with variance in the PhILR Euclidean distances.
source: Consistent with prior studies (Falony et al., 2016), PERMANOVA analysis of our full 16S-seq data set revealed that diabetes (Forslund et al., 2015), age (Ghosh et al., 2020), metformin use (Wu et al., 2017), and statin intake (Vieira-Silva et al., 2020) were significantly associated with variance in the PhILR Euclidean distances (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Statin intake was significantly associated with variance in the PhILR Euclidean distances.
source: Consistent with prior studies (Falony et al., 2016), PERMANOVA analysis of our full 16S-seq data set revealed that diabetes (Forslund et al., 2015), age (Ghosh et al., 2020), metformin use (Wu et al., 2017), and statin intake (Vieira-Silva et al., 2020) were significantly associated with variance in the PhILR Euclidean distances (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Metagenomic sequencing confirmed significant associations with ethnicity and statin use.
source: Metagenomic sequencing of the IDEO cohort with subsequent PERMANOVA analysis confirmed significant associations with ethnicity and statin use
evidence: This finding is stated in the text based on metagenomic analysis.

claim: Metagenomic sequencing revealed significant associations with HOMA-IR and BMI.
source: Metagenomic sequencing of the IDEO cohort with subsequent PERMANOVA analysis confirmed significant associations with ethnicity and statin use, while also highlighting significant associations with HOMA-IR and BMI (Figure 2B), consistent with prior reports (Liu et al., 2017; Zouiouich et al., 2021).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2B.

claim: Only triglyceride levels were significantly different between lean EA and W subjects, but this trend did not survive multiple testing correction.
source: While several factors linked to body composition were different between obese EA and W subjects using a nominal p-value, only triglyceride levels were significantly different between lean EA and W subjects and this trend did not survive multiple testing correction (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text with reference to supplementary data.

claim: There was no significant difference in the proportion of subjects born in the United States between ethnicities (75% W, 54.5% EA; p=0.15).
source: There was no significant difference in the proportion of subjects born in the United States between ethnicities (75% W, 54.5% EA; p=0.15, Pearson's χ2 test).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text based on demographic analysis.

claim: There was no significant difference in the geographical distance between birth location and San Francisco between ethnicities.
source: There was also no significant difference in the geographical distance between birth location and San Francisco [W median 2,318 (2.2–6,906) miles; EA median 1,986 (2.2–6,906) miles; p=0.69, Wilcoxon rank-sum test]
evidence: This finding is stated in the text based on geographical analysis.

claim: There was no significant difference in the amount of time spent in the San Francisco Bay Area at the time of sampling between ethnicities.
source: or the amount of time spent in the San Francisco Bay Area at the time of sampling [W median 270 (8.00–741) months; EA median 282.5 (8.50–777) months; p=0.42, Wilcoxon rank-sum test].
evidence: This finding is stated in the text based on demographic analysis.

claim: No significant differences in short-term dietary intake were detected between ethnicities.
source: Surprisingly, we did not detect any significant differences in either short- (Supplementary file 1F) or long-term (Supplementary file 1G) dietary intake between ethnicities.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text with reference to supplementary data.

claim: No significant differences in long-term dietary intake were detected between ethnicities.
source: Surprisingly, we did not detect any significant differences in either short- (Supplementary file 1F) or long-term (Supplementary file 1G) dietary intake between ethnicities.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text with reference to supplementary data.

claim: Procrustes analysis did not reveal any significant associations between dietary intake and gut microbial community structure.
source: Consistent with this, procrustes analysis did not reveal any significant associations between dietary intake and gut microbial community structure: procrustes p=0.280 (DHQIII) and p=0.080 (ASA24) relative to PhILR transformed 16S-seq ASV data.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text based on procrustes analysis.

claim: The Spearman Mantel statistic was non-significant for the association between dietary intake and gut microbial community structure.
source: The Spearman Mantel statistic was also non-significant [r=0.0524, p=0.243 (DHQIII) and r=−0.0173, p=0.590 (ASA24)], relative to PhILR transformed 16S-seq ASV data.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text based on Mantel test analysis.

claim: 12 ASVs and 7 metagenomic species were associated with dietary intake in lean W individuals.
source: Despite the lack of an overall association between reported dietary intake and the gut microbiota, we were able to identify 12 ASVs and 7 metagenomic species associated with dietary intake in lean W individuals (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 3A.

claim: 20 significant species-level associations with dietary intake were detected in lean EA subjects.
source: We also detected 20 significant species-level associations in lean EA subjects (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 3B.

claim: There were no overlapping associations between ethnicities in dietary intake-microbiota relationships.
source: There were no overlapping associations between ethnicities.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text based on comparison of dietary associations.

claim: Clear trends in ethnic group composition across ZIP codes in the IDEO cohort were mirrored by the 2018 US census data (Pearson r=0.52, p=0.026).
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we found clear trends in ethnic group composition across ZIP codes in the IDEO cohort (Figure 6A and B) that were mirrored by the 2018 US census data (Pearson r=0.52, p=0.026 for neighborhoods with greater than 50% W subjects; Figure 6D).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6A, B, and D.

claim: Obese individuals from both ethnicities and lean W subjects tended to live closer to the center of San Francisco relative to lean EA subjects.
source: Obese individuals from both ethnicities and lean W subjects tended to live closer to the center of San Francisco relative to lean EA subjects (Figure 6C).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6C.

claim: Distance between the current ZIP code and the center of San Francisco was associated with gut microbial community structure.
source: Distance between the current ZIP code and the center of San Francisco and duration of residency within San Francisco were both associated with gut microbial community structure (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6E.

claim: Duration of residency within San Francisco was associated with gut microbial community structure.
source: Distance between the current ZIP code and the center of San Francisco and duration of residency within San Francisco were both associated with gut microbial community structure (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6F.

claim: The association between the current address and the gut microbiota was robust to the central point used, as evidenced by using the Bay Bridge as the central reference point (p=0.008, rho=0.394).
source: The association between the current address and the gut microbiota was robust to the central point used, as evidenced by using the Bay Bridge as the central reference point (p=0.008, rho=0.394, Spearman correlation).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text based on alternative geographical analysis.

claim: Significant differences in gut microbial community structure were detected between recipient mice transplanted with microbiota from EA compared to W donors on the LFPP diet.
source: Despite maintaining the genetically identical recipient mice on the same autoclaved LFPP diet, we detected significant differences in gut microbial community structure (Figure 7A)
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 7A showing the PCoA plot.

claim: Bacterial richness was significantly lower in recipient mice transplanted with microbiota from EA compared to W donors on the LFPP diet.
source: Despite maintaining the genetically identical recipient mice on the same autoclaved LFPP diet, we detected significant differences in gut microbial community structure (Figure 7A), bacterial richness (Figure 7C)
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 7C.

claim: Bacteroides abundance was significantly higher in recipient mice transplanted with microbiota from EA compared to W donors on the LFPP diet.
source: These differences recapitulated key aspects of the gut microbiota observed in the IDEO cohort, including significantly lower bacterial richness (Figure 7C) and higher abundance of Bacteroides (Figure 7D and E) in recipient mice transplanted with microbiota from EA compared to W donors.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 7D and E.

claim: Significant differences in gut microbial community structure were detected between recipient mice transplanted with microbiota from EA compared to W donors on the HFHS diet.
source: This experiment replicated our original findings on the LFPP diet, including significantly altered gut microbial community structure between ethnicities (Figure 7F)
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 7F showing the PCoA plot.

claim: Bacterial richness was significantly increased in mice receiving W donor microbiota on the HFHS diet.
source: This experiment replicated our original findings on the LFPP diet, including significantly altered gut microbial community structure between ethnicities (Figure 7F), significantly increased richness in mice receiving W donor microbiota (Figure 7H)
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 7H.

claim: There was a trend toward higher levels of Bacteroides in mice receiving the gut microbiotas of EA donors on the HFHS diet.
source: This experiment replicated our original findings on the LFPP diet, including significantly altered gut microbial community structure between ethnicities (Figure 7F), significantly increased richness in mice receiving W donor microbiota (Figure 7H), and a trend toward higher levels of Bacteroides in mice receiving the gut microbiotas of EA donors (Figure 7I and J).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 7I and J.

claim: The variance explained by ethnicity was lower in mice fed the HFHS diet (R2=0.126) than the LFPP diet (R2=0.384).
source: Of note, the variance explained by ethnicity was lower in mice fed the HFHS diet (R2=0.126) than the LFPP diet (R2=0.384)
evidence: This finding is stated in the text based on comparison of ADONIS results.

claim: Excessive fat and sugar consumption may serve to diminish the signal otherwise associated with ethnicity in the context of human obesity.
source: potentially suggesting that in the context of human obesity, excessive fat and sugar consumption may serve to diminish the signal otherwise associated with ethnicity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data comparing LFPP and HFHS diets.

claim: There was no difference between ethnic groups in the efficiency of engraftment in gnotobiotic mice.
source: As expected (Nayak et al., 2021; Turnbaugh et al., 2009; Walter et al., 2020), the input donor microbiota was distinct from that of the recipient mice (Figure 7B and G); however, there was no difference between ethnic groups in the efficiency of engraftment (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: In a pooled analysis of all gnotobiotic experiments, ethnicity and diet were both significantly associated with variations in the gut microbiota.
source: In a pooled analysis of all gnotobiotic experiments accounting for one donor for multiple recipient mice, ethnicity and diet were both significantly associated with variations in the gut microbiota (Figure 7—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: LFPP fed mice that received W donor microbiota had significantly increased adiposity relative to LFPP fed mice that received the EA donor microbiota.
source: LFPP fed mice that received W donor microbiota had significantly increased adiposity in conjunction with decreased lean mass, relative to LFPP fed mice that received the EA donor microbiota (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 8A-C.

claim: LFPP fed mice that received W donor microbiota had significantly decreased lean mass relative to LFPP fed mice that received the EA donor microbiota.
source: LFPP fed mice that received W donor microbiota had significantly increased adiposity in conjunction with decreased lean mass, relative to LFPP fed mice that received the EA donor microbiota (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 8A-C.

claim: The trends in body composition observed on the LFPP diet were mirrored in recipient mice fed the HFHS diet but did not reach statistical significance.
source: Although these trends were mirrored in recipient mice that fed the HFHS diet (Figure 8E–G), they did not reach statistical significance.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 8E-G.

claim: There were no significant differences in glucose tolerance between groups in either LFPP or HFHS experiments.
source: There were no significant differences in glucose tolerance in either experiment (Figure 8D and H).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 8D and H.

claim: Dietary input may mask the metabolic consequences of ethnicity-associated differences in the gut microbiota.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that dietary input may mask the metabolic consequences of ethnicity-associated differences in the gut microbiota.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the body composition and glucose tolerance data.

claim: Even in a given geographic location, there remain stable long-lasting microbial signatures of ethnicity.
source: Despite the potential for immigration to erase some of the geographically specific aspects of gut microbiome structure (Vangay et al., 2018), our study suggests that even in a given geographic location, there remain stable long-lasting microbial signatures of ethnicity, as revealed here for W and EA residents of the San Francisco Bay Area.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the study findings.

claim: In lean individuals within the IDEO cohort, differences in the gut microbiota appear to be independent of immigration status, host phenotype, or dietary intake.
source: In lean individuals within the IDEO cohort, these differences appear to be independent of immigration status, host phenotype, or dietary intake.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the study findings.

claim: Variations in host genetics are not necessary to maintain ethnicity-associated signatures in the gut microbiota, at least over short timescales.
source: Our experiments using inbred germ-free mice support the stability of ethnicity-associated differences in the gut microbiota on both the LFPP and HFHS diets, while also demonstrating that variations in host genetics are not necessary to maintain these signatures, at least over short timescales.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the mouse experiments.

claim: Current location may reflect subtle differences in dietary intake that are hard to capture using validated nutritional surveys.
source: Current location may reflect subtle differences in dietary intake (e.g., ethnic foods, food sources, or phytochemical contents) that are hard to capture using the validated nutritional surveys employed here (Garduño-Diaz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the discussion to explain the geographical findings.

claim: Alternative hypotheses for the role of current location include biogeographical patterns in microbial dispersion.
source: Alternative hypotheses include biogeographical patterns in microbial dispersion (Martiny et al., 2006)
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis stated in the discussion.

claim: Alternative hypotheses for the role of current location include a role for socioeconomic factors, which are correlated with neighborhood.
source: Alternative hypotheses include biogeographical patterns in microbial dispersion (Martiny et al., 2006) or a role for socioeconomic factors, which are correlated with neighborhood (Kakar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis stated in the discussion.

claim: Ethnicity-associated differences in the gut microbiota are stronger in lean individuals.
source: Surprisingly, our findings demonstrate that ethnicity-associated differences in the gut microbiota are stronger in lean individuals.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the stratified analysis.

claim: Established obesity or its associated dietary patterns can overwrite long-lasting microbial signatures.
source: Obese individuals did not exhibit as clear a difference in the gut microbiota between ethnic groups, either suggesting that established obesity or its associated dietary patterns can overwrite long-lasting microbial signatures.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the discussion to explain the findings in obese individuals.

claim: There could be a shared ethnicity-independent microbiome type that predisposes individuals to obesity.
source: Alternatively, there could be a shared ethnicity-independent microbiome type that predisposes individuals to obesity.
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis stated in the discussion.

claim: EA subjects had increased Firmicutes, which has been previously linked to obesity and its associated metabolic diseases.
source: In humans, we did find multiple signals that have been previously linked to obesity and its associated metabolic diseases in EA individuals, including increased Firmicutes (Basolo et al., 2020; Bisanz et al., 2019)
evidence: This finding is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: EA subjects had decreased A. muciniphila, which has been previously linked to obesity and its associated metabolic diseases.
source: In humans, we did find multiple signals that have been previously linked to obesity and its associated metabolic diseases in EA individuals, including increased Firmicutes (Basolo et al., 2020; Bisanz et al., 2019), decreased A. muciniphila (Depommier et al., 2019; Plovier et al., 2017)
evidence: This finding is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: EA subjects had decreased diversity, which has been previously linked to obesity and its associated metabolic diseases.
source: In humans, we did find multiple signals that have been previously linked to obesity and its associated metabolic diseases in EA individuals, including increased Firmicutes (Basolo et al., 2020; Bisanz et al., 2019), decreased A. muciniphila (Depommier et al., 2019; Plovier et al., 2017), decreased diversity (Turnbaugh et al., 2008)
evidence: This finding is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: EA subjects had increased acetate, which has been previously linked to obesity and its associated metabolic diseases.
source: In humans, we did find multiple signals that have been previously linked to obesity and its associated metabolic diseases in EA individuals, including increased Firmicutes (Basolo et al., 2020; Bisanz et al., 2019), decreased A. muciniphila (Depommier et al., 2019; Plovier et al., 2017), decreased diversity (Turnbaugh et al., 2008), and increased acetate (Perry et al., 2016; Turnbaugh et al., 2006).
evidence: This finding is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: EA subjects had higher levels of Bacteroidota and Bacteroides, which have been linked to improved metabolic health.
source: Yet EA subjects also had higher levels of Bacteroidota and Bacteroides, which have been linked to improved metabolic health (Johnson et al., 2017).
evidence: This finding is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The recipient mice may have lost some of the microbial features of ethnicity relevant to host metabolic disease.
source: These seemingly contradictory findings may suggest that the recipient mice lost some of the microbial features of ethnicity relevant to host metabolic disease
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the discussion to explain the contradictory findings.

claim: The microbiome may act in a beneficial manner to counteract other ethnicity-associated factors driving disease.
source: or alternatively that the microbiome acts in a beneficial manner to counteract other ethnicity-associated factors driving disease.
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis stated in the discussion.

claim: Propionate may either exacerbate or protect from aspects of metabolic syndrome.
source: The consequences of elevated intestinal propionate levels are unclear given the seemingly conflicting evidence in the literature that propionate may either exacerbate (Tirosh et al., 2019) or protect from (Lu et al., 2016) aspects of metabolic syndrome.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Clinical data suggests that circulating propionate may be more relevant for disease than fecal levels.
source: Clinical data suggests that circulating propionate may be more relevant for disease than fecal levels (Müller et al., 2019)
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Isobutyrate has prior links to dietary intake but no association with obesity.
source: Isobutyrate is even less well-characterized, with prior links to dietary intake (Berding and Donovan, 2018) but no association with obesity (Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The IDEO cohort was relatively small at the time of this analysis (n=46 individuals).
source: Due to the investment of resources into ensuring a high level of phenotypic information on each cohort member coupled to the restricted geographical catchment area, the IDEO cohort was relatively small at the time of this analysis (n=46 individuals).
evidence: This limitation is stated in the discussion.

claim: The current study only focused on two of the major ethnicities in the San Francisco Bay Area.
source: The current study only focused on two of the major ethnicities in the San Francisco Bay Area.
evidence: This limitation is stated in the discussion.

claim: Stool samples were collected at a single time point and analyzed in a cross-sectional manner.
source: Stool samples were collected at a single time point and analyzed in a cross-sectional manner.
evidence: This limitation is stated in the discussion.

claim: All mouse experiments were performed in wild-type adult males.
source: Our mouse experiments were all performed in wild-type adult males.
evidence: This limitation is stated in the discussion.
